source: Toprank Review Academy (TRA) Nursing Module – Complete Handout

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: Which drug may close a PDA in a premature infant?
questions.rationale: Prostaglandin inhibitors such as indomethacin or ibuprofen may close the ductus; PGE1 keeps it open.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, PDA (PDF p. 226)
questions.quote: Ibuprofen or Indomethacin, prostaglandin inhibitors, may be administered to close a patent ductu

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: Bounding radial pulses with absent femoral pulses suggest:
questions.rationale: This is the pathognomonic sign of coarctation; upper-body BP is high.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Coarctation (PDF p. 226)
questions.quote: Bounding radial pulse and absent femoral pulse (pathognomonic sign)

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: Which defects make up tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.rationale: Tetralogy: pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, overriding aorta, VSD.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Tetralogy of Fallot (PDF p. 227)
questions.quote: Overriding aorta

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: A child with tetralogy of Fallot has a hypercyanotic spell. How is the infant positioned?
questions.rationale: Knee-chest (or squatting) increases systemic resistance and pulmonary blood flow.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Tetralogy of Fallot (PDF p. 228)
questions.quote: knee-chest, squatting for preschool or older children

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: Which finding is typical of cyanotic heart disease?
questions.rationale: Cyanotic defects cause central cyanosis, clubbing, squatting, polycythemia (high Hct), and poor growth.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Cyanotic Defects (PDF p. 227)
questions.quote: Clubbing of fingers

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: Why is PGE1 infused in an infant with tricuspid atresia?
questions.rationale: PGE1 keeps the ductus arteriosus open to maintain oxygenation until surgery.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Tricuspid Atresia (PDF p. 228)
questions.quote: An IV infusion of PGE1 is begun to ensure that the ductus remains open

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: A newborn becomes cyanotic when feeding but pink when crying. Suspect:
questions.rationale: Infants breathe through the nose; crying opens the mouth airway, relieving cyanosis.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Choanal Atresia (PDF p. 228)
questions.quote: Cyanosis during feeding

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: After tonsillectomy, which sign suggests hemorrhage?
questions.rationale: Frequent swallowing may indicate bleeding; turn the child to the side and notify the doctor.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Tonsillectomy (PDF p. 229)
questions.quote: frequent swallowing may indicate hemorrhage

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: Which fluid is best after tonsillectomy?
questions.rationale: Give clear, cool, non-citrus, non-carbonated fluids; avoid milk (coats throat) and red liquids (look like blood).
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Tonsillectomy (PDF p. 229)
questions.quote: Provide clear, cool, non-citrus and noncarbonated fluids

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: How is a child positioned after tonsillectomy?
questions.rationale: Prone or side-lying facilitates drainage of secretions.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Tonsillectomy (PDF p. 229)
questions.quote: Position the child prone or side-lying to facilitate drainage

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: A child with epiglottitis drools and sits in a tripod position. What should the nurse AVOID?
questions.rationale: Never visualize the epiglottis with a tongue blade or take a throat culture; it may cause complete obstruction.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Epiglottitis (PDF p. 229)
questions.quote: Never attempt to visualize the epiglottis directly with a tongue blade or obtain a throat culture

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: Rheumatic fever usually follows a strep throat by:
questions.rationale: Rheumatic fever presents 2–6 weeks after an untreated group A strep infection; glomerulonephritis 5–21 days.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Tonsillitis (PDF p. 229)
questions.quote: Rheumatic fever presents 2 to 6 weeks following an untreated or partially treated group

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: During which situation should chest physiotherapy be withheld in asthma?
questions.rationale: CPT is not recommended during an acute exacerbation.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Asthma (PDF p. 230)
questions.quote: Chest physiotherapy is not recommended during an acute exacerbation

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: Asthma that persists despite vigorous treatment is called:
questions.rationale: Status asthmaticus is a medical emergency that can cause respiratory failure.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Status Asthmaticus (PDF p. 230)
questions.quote: Child displays respiratory distress despite vigorous treatment measures

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: How is an infant with cleft lip fed before repair?
questions.rationale: Hold upright, use an enlarged nipple, direct formula to the side and back of the mouth, and allow rests.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Cleft Lip/Palate (PDF p. 230)
questions.quote: Direct the formula to the side and back of the mouth

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: After cleft LIP repair, which position is AVOIDED?
questions.rationale: Avoid prone after cheiloplasty to prevent rubbing the suture line on the mattress.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Cheiloplasty (PDF p. 231)
questions.quote: avoid prone position

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: After cleft PALATE repair, what should be avoided?
questions.rationale: Avoid oral suction, straws, and sharp objects near the palate; use elbow restraints.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Palatoplasty (PDF p. 231)
questions.quote: Avoid oral suction or placing objects in the mouth

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: A 5-week-old has projectile, non-bilious vomiting and an olive-shaped mass. What is suspected?
questions.rationale: Pyloric stenosis: projectile non-bilious vomiting at 4–6 weeks, visible peristalsis, olive mass.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Pyloric Stenosis (PDF p. 231)
questions.quote: Olive shaped mass in the epigastrium just right of the umbilicus

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: An infant on IV fluids only for pyloric stenosis needs:
questions.rationale: Infants receiving only IV fluids need a pacifier to meet sucking needs.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Pyloric Stenosis (PDF p. 231)
questions.quote: An infant who is receiving only IV fluid generally needs a pacifier

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: Which dairy food is usually better tolerated in lactose intolerance?
questions.rationale: Yogurt and hard cheese contain less lactose; milk is taken with food in small amounts.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Lactose Intolerance (PDF p. 232)
questions.quote: Encourage consumption of hard cheese, cottage cheese, or yogurt

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: Which grains are ALLOWED in celiac disease?
questions.rationale: Avoid BROW (barley, rye, oats, wheat); rice, corn, and millet are substitutes.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Celiac Disease (PDF p. 232)
questions.quote: substituting corn, rice, and millet as grain sources

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: A 'double bubble' sign on abdominal x-ray suggests:
questions.rationale: Duodenal atresia shows a double bubble with early bilious vomiting.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Duodenal Atresia (PDF p. 232)
questions.quote: the so-called “double bubble” sig

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: A newborn passes no stool in 48 hours and later has ribbon-like stools. Suspect:
questions.rationale: Hirschsprung's (aganglionic megacolon) causes delayed meconium, ribbon stools, and abdominal distention.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Hirschsprung's Disease (PDF p. 233)
questions.quote: No bowel movement in the first 48 hours of life

questions.subject: NP II
questions.topic: Care of the At-Risk and Sick Child
questions.stem: After Hirschsprung's surgery, what is measured daily?
questions.rationale: Abdominal girth is measured daily; NPO until bowel sounds or flatus return.
questions.source: TRA Nursing Module, Hirschsprung's Disease (PDF p. 233)
questions.quote: Measure abdominal girth daily and PRN
